title: Advanced Programming and Parallel Computing
text:
1 Preface
This site is the support for the “Advanced Programming and Parallel Computing” module of the MIASHS master’s degree (Mathematics and Computer Science Applied to the Humanities and Social Sciences), Université Paul-Valéry Montpellier 3.
The module covers six families of techniques: asynchronous programming, inter-process communication and locks, distributed computing (Dask, Ray), SIMD, GPU and WebGPU.
This module rests on a self-directed, co-constructed learning design: two tracks are offered, one with an AI tutor that you design and improve yourself, the other with classic learning from the resources. The technical objectives are identical; only the learning process differs. You will find all the details on the Teaching design page.
You can browse the site like a book: use the table of contents on the left. Before the first session, follow the Prerequisites page to install your tooling.

title: 2  Prerequisites
text:
2.1 Editor: Zed
For this module you need two basic tools (a code editor and a Python environment manager), plus, for Track A, access to a language model. All the options below are free; the effective limits of each offer are given (verified on 25/08/2026).
Zed is the editor used in the labs. It is free, fast, and includes a code assistant (Agent) that can be connected to any OpenAI-compatible API, including the free offers described below.

title: 2  Prerequisites
text:
Installation: https://zed.dev/ (macOS, Linux, Windows).
No configuration is needed to write code; only the Agent panel must be connected to a model (see Track A tooling).
(Optional) a free Zed account enables collaborative editing in channels (see Collaborative editing).

title: 2  Prerequisites
text:
2.2 Python environment management with uv
uv is the recommended Python environment manager. It installs the environment and packages in the current directory.
See the installation documentation for your platform. Then:
uv init          # creates an environment in the current directory
uv add package   # adds a package (replace package by its name)
Run a script with a one-off dependency:
uv run --with dependance script.py

title: 2  Prerequisites
section: 2.3 Track A tooling: an AI tutor
text:
2.3 Track A tooling: an AI tutor
Track A requires access to a large language model (LLM). Three options, all free, depending on your hardware and preferences; the kick-off survey distributed in session will help us calibrate this choice.

2.3.1 Option 1 — OpenRouter API (recommended)
OpenRouter is an aggregator: one API key gives access to dozens of models (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek, gpt-oss, Nemotron…) through a single OpenAI-compatible API.

Create an account at https://openrouter.ai/ (email or GitHub, no credit card).
Generate an API key (the Keys page of your account).
In Zed, add an OpenAI-compatible provider:

URL: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
Key: your OpenRouter key
Model: open the Free Models collection and copy the identifier of a model whose ID ends with :free (as of 25/08/2026: 17 models, e.g. z-ai/glm-5.2:free, cohere/north-mini-code:free, google/gemma-4-31b-it:free, nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free). The catalog changes often: if a model disappears, the Free Models page lists the replacement. You can configure several models and switch from one to the other in the Agent panel.


Effective limits (25/08/2026). The cap applies to the number of requests, not to tokens:



Limit

The daily quota rises to 1,000/day as soon as the account has bought at least $10 of credits once (credits never expire); the increase stays even if the balance drops back to zero. A single $10 top-up on a class account is therefore enough.
Free models are served at low priority: waiting may occur at peak hours, and the :free model catalog changes regularly (some disappear, others appear); hence the value of configuring several models.
Failed requests (429 = limit reached) count towards the daily quota.
In tokens, OpenRouter imposes no global quota on free models: the size of a request is bounded by the model’s context window (as of 25/08/2026: from 64k to 1M tokens, e.g. z-ai/glm-5.2:free in 256k, nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free in 1M) and the throughput (tokens/min) is set by each provider, often reduced at peak hours. Only the request counters (20/min, 50/day) are authoritative at the OpenRouter level.
Check the data policy of each provider: some free endpoints may train on your exchanges. Avoid sending sensitive data to them.


If each student creates their own OpenRouter account (2 minutes), each gets their own 50 requests/day; this is the simplest and safest option for a class.



2.3.2 Option 2 — Mistral API (free key)
Mistral “La Plateforme” offers a free Experiment plan: access to all models (Mistral Small, Medium, Large, Codestral, Magistral…), no credit card, but with a phone verification.

Create an account at https://console.mistral.ai/home and grab an API key. A valid phone number is required; warn the instructor if this is a problem.
In Zed, add an OpenAI-compatible provider:

URL: https://api.mistral.ai/v1
Key: your Mistral key
Model: mistral-small-latest (reasoning enabled with reasoning_effort: "high", see the troubleshooting below) or mistral-medium-3-5 (more powerful, same mechanism).


Effective limits (Experiment plan): approximate and unpublished figures (exact in the console, Limits section); about 1 billion tokens/month, ~500,000 tokens/min per model and ~1 request/s per API key (2 req/min according to some sources). The detailed quotas vary by model group (e.g. magistral: 20,000 tokens/min, 10 req/min). This plan is meant for experimentation, not production.
Data: free-plan requests may be used to train Mistral models (retention ~30 days, cf. their privacy policy); do not send sensitive code or exchanges.
For reasoning models, see the troubleshooting below.


2.3.3 Option 3 — Local model (if your machine allows it)
If you have at least ~16 GB of RAM (or a dedicated GPU with ~6 GB of VRAM) and ~8 GB of free disk space, you can run a local model like Qwen 3.5-4B (≈5.5 GB quantized) with llama.cpp or LM Studio. A local model works offline and without any account; Zed connects to it as an OpenAI-compatible provider (http://localhost:11434/v1). The kick-off survey (distributed in session) is precisely used to know who can run one.

If your machine is modest: don’t worry. Option 1 or 2 (free API) is enough to follow Track A. Track B, for its part, requires no AI tool at all.

title: 2  Prerequisites
section: 2.4 Troubleshooting: Mistral’s reasoning (“thinking”) does not show
text:
2.4 Troubleshooting: Mistral’s reasoning (“thinking”) does not show
Three frequent causes:

You use a model that does not reason, or an outdated name. Reasoning is now adjustable and is triggered by the reasoning_effort parameter:

Concerned models: mistral-small-latest and mistral-medium-3-5; they think only if you send reasoning_effort: "high" (default = "none": no thinking).
The magistral-*-latest names (“native” reasoning, always on) are deprecated at Mistral (25/08/2026): magistral-small-latest now resolves to mistral-small-latest, with adjustable reasoning. Prefer mistral-small-latest with reasoning_effort: "high".
The other models (Large, Codestral…) have no reasoning mode: sending them reasoning_effort causes an HTTP 422 error.

The parameter is misplaced. reasoning_effort is a root-level field of the Chat Completions request body (not in extra_body, not in a message).
The response format changes. With reasoning_effort: "high", message.content becomes a list of chunks (ThinkChunk for the trace, then TextChunk for the answer) instead of a string. Code that reads content as a string “shows nothing” or crashes. Two useful details:

In streaming, delta.content changes shape: a list of ThinkChunk during the reflection, then a mixed list (end of ThinkChunk + first TextChunk) at the transition, then a plain string for the final answer. Code that always expects the same type “shows nothing” without crashing.
Be tolerant about chunking: depending on the model, the answer may contain empty ThinkChunks interleaved within TextChunks (a bug reported on magistral-medium-latest). Keep only the text of the TextChunks and ignore the rest.
In multi-turn, send back in the history the complete assistant message (with its trace): removing the ThinkChunk of previous turns degrades quality noticeably.


Minimal working example (Python mistralai SDK):
from mistralai import Mistral
from mistralai.models import TextChunk

client = Mistral(api_key="YOUR_KEY")
resp = client.chat.complete(
    model="mistral-small-latest",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the concept of a lock."}],
    reasoning_effort="high",
)
content = resp.choices[0].message.content
if isinstance(content, str):
    print(content)  # reasoning_effort="none": plain string
else:
    for chunk in content:
        if isinstance(chunk, TextChunk):
            print(chunk.text, end="")  # ThinkChunks (trace) are ignored
Same in curl (the key in an environment variable MISTRAL_API_KEY):
curl https://api.mistral.ai/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MISTRAL_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"mistral-small-latest","reasoning_effort":"high","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain the concept of a lock."}]}'
In Zed: declare Mistral as an OpenAI-compatible provider (https://api.mistral.ai/v1) and, for the model, set reasoning_effort to "high" in its configuration (available_models in the Agent settings). This setting activates the thinking and asks Zed to display the trace in the panel. On older versions of Zed, reasoning_effort could not be forwarded for OpenAI-compatible providers (bug fixed since); update Zed if the thinking does not show. Mistral returns the trace in message.content (chunks), not as a dedicated field: a tool that expects a plain string may display “nothing”. To see the trace in all circumstances, use a script (as above) or Mistral Le Chat.

Zed supports collaborative editing: a participant opens a channel (public or private) and the others join it with the link. Sessions may use this feature or the module’s Discord room (the exact channel will be given in the lab).

title: 2  Prerequisites
text:
2.6 Running multiprocessing/asyncio in Jupyter
Under macOS, multiprocessing requires the spawn method in Jupyter notebooks; a fix that requires kernel-specific settings. The most robust approach is to run your scripts with uv run rather than in a notebook cell; the details are covered in the lab if needed.

title: 3  The pedagogical design
text:
3.1 The general idea
This page explains the design of this module: how you will learn and why this choice was made. Read it carefully: everything for the semester follows from it.
Knowledge is built in interaction: with the people around you, and with the documents and tools you work with. This module puts you at the center of your learning: you design part of your own path, and you observe how you learn.
Concretely, the idea has three parts:

title: 3  The pedagogical design
text:
Autonomous, co-constructed learning: you write a learning plan and follow it, with regular support.
A “learning by teaching” setup: by configuring an AI tutor that must teach you correctly, you are forced to master the material. You cannot ask a machine to teach a concept you do not understand yourself.
A critical approach: AI has documented limitations (hallucinations, over-reliance, superficial uses, unequal access). The course makes them an object of work and analysis.

title: 3  The pedagogical design
text:
3.2 Two tracks, identical objectives
The technical objectives are the same for everyone. Only the way of learning differs.

3.2.1 Track A: Socratic AI tutor

You write a structured learning plan.
You design a system prompt that configures a chatbot as a Socratic tutor: it does not give answers, it questions, guides, and makes you articulate your thinking.
You interact daily with this tutor and iterate on the system prompt based on the quality of the exchanges.
You keep a logbook that includes the tutor’s full conversations.



3.2.2 Track B: classic learning

You write the same kind of learning plan.
You work from the available resources: this site, the documentation, books, tutorials, last year’s course.
You keep a logbook of your autonomous work, and you demonstrate mastery through live-coding (board work or an individual session with the instructor).



3.2.3 Switching tracks
You can start in one track and switch to the other during the semester, as long as the choice is justified and explained in your report. The flexibility is deliberate: it lets each student find the way they learn best, and it is part of the module’s reflective work.

This is a parallel-programming course whose learning process partly relies on tools whose effects you will learn to master or work around.

title: 3  The pedagogical design
text:
3.3 Reciprocal observation
You will write a comparative report that blends two parts:

Reflective part: analysis of your own learning process. Which strategies worked, where difficulties appeared, how you resolved them.
Observational part: observation of the students in the other track. How do they learn? Does the approach seem effective, and on what criteria? What reactions does it trigger in you (envy, wariness) and why?

Track A students observe group B to understand what motivates the choice to do without AI and to justify why their own use is not mere over-reliance. Track B students observe group A to analyze the learning processes at work and to be better equipped to move through a professional world where AI is omnipresent.
Mid-semester, a cross-review session (anonymous reading of the reports and collective discussion) pools these observations. The goal is not to decide who is right, but to develop an informed relationship with technology.

title: 3  The pedagogical design
text:
3.4 Working modes
The module is designed so that each student finds a format that suits them. Every working mode counts as much as the others; no choice is interpreted as lesser commitment.

3.4.1 Solo work

With the AI tutor (Track A): asynchronous dialogue at your own pace, where you can rephrase, go back, and think before answering.
With the resources (Track B): documentation, books, tutorials, previous courses.
The logbook, under any circumstances, is your main channel of written expression.



3.4.2 Pair work

Reciprocal observation pairs work through written exchange (journals read crosswise, asynchronous comments) or orally (a 15–20 minute interview), at the participants’ choice.
The final project can be done solo or in pairs (communication arrangements defined by the pair itself).



3.4.3 Speaking up in group
Five channels are equivalent:

Spontaneous oral speaking up;
Announced oral speaking up: you signal in advance that you want to intervene;
Asynchronous written contribution: written before the session (forum, shared document), read or projected by the instructor or a peer;
Synchronous written contribution: written during the session (chat, collaborative document);
Contribution by artifact: a diagram, code, or screenshot that carries your contribution without you having to defend it orally.

The instructor gives non-oral contributions the same weight in the discussion as oral ones.


3.4.4 Board work
“Board work” (demonstration, live-coding) is a moment with high social stakes. Four equivalent modes:

Classic board work;
Individual session with the instructor;
Asynchronous recording (a 5–10 minute video, projected anonymously if you wish);
Demonstration by artifact (commented code, architecture diagram, debugging trace).

Golden rule: no one is put in public difficulty. If you want an alternative, it is offered without justification and without penalty.


3.4.5 Signals and think time

The instructor leaves a think time (1–2 minutes) before asking for an answer.
A discreet overload signal (card, agreed gesture, message in the chat) lets you ask for a pause, and the request is respected without public comment.

title: 3  The pedagogical design
text:
3.7 The safeguards (why they are there)

Track A: the tutor’s full conversations in the logbook serve as objective traces. If the tutor gives a wrong answer, you must document how you detected it and corrected it. That is exactly the kind of skill the module wants to develop.
Track B: the proof of mastery is more direct (live-coding, individual session), and the documentation load is lighter.

title: 3  The pedagogical design
text:
3.8 To go further

The page Designing an AI tutor details the work of block 2 (Track A).
The page Planning your learning details the learning contract (all tracks).
A few basic readings: dialogic pedagogy and co-construction (Vygotski, Freire, Bovill), documented limits of AI in education (hallucinations, over-reliance, unequal access). The references are listed at the end of the site.

title: 4  Designing an AI tutor
text:
4.1 Why configure the tutor?
A “raw” chatbot is often a poor teacher: it gives answers directly, which shortcuts the construction of understanding, and it hallucinates, producing false claims with confidence.
A good Socratic tutor, by contrast:
To configure this behavior, you must understand the material as well as the pedagogy: that is the learning by teaching principle. If you cannot tell a good explanation from a bad one, you will not be able to correct your tutor.

title: 4  Designing an AI tutor
4  Designing an AI tutor
section: 4.2 The anatomy of a system prompt
text:
4.2 The anatomy of a system prompt
A system prompt is the text that sets the chatbot’s behavior. It is built from blocks:

Role: who the tutor is, for what audience. E.g.: > “You are a Socratic Python programming tutor for a master’s student in applied computer > science. Your goal is to help them understand asynchronous programming concepts, never > to do the work for them.”
Method: how it teaches. E.g.: > “You progress with short questions. You never give a solution directly: you guide the > student step by step. When they make a mistake, you do not give the correction: you > ask a question that makes them reflect on their error.”
Anti-cheating rules: what is forbidden. E.g.: > “You never provide the complete code of an exercise. You can give a skeleton, a hint, > or point to the documentation. You politely refuse if the student insists.”
Handling hallucinations: how it manages uncertainty. E.g.: > “If you are not sure of an answer, say so explicitly and offer to check the > documentation. Clearly flag the points of the documentation that you are inventing.”
Tone and format: how it expresses itself. E.g.: > “You answer in French, concisely and encouragingly. You check understanding before > moving on.”
Context (optional): the material to teach. You can provide an excerpt from the course material, a chapter outline, or precise learning objectives.

title: 4  Designing an AI tutor
text:
4.3 The iteration process
A system prompt is never “finished”. Work loop:

Write a v1 (blocks above).
Test on typical module exercises: does the tutor give the right amount of help? Does it resist the request for a solution? Does it spot an error?
Observe the conversations: where is the tutor too directive? too vague? What did it invent?
Iterate: rephrase, constrain, add an example dialogue to imitate or to avoid in the prompt.
Record: keep track of the prompt versions and the reason for each change. This is valuable material for your reflective report.


Logically, the prompt can even start with “do not open the topic with…”. In practice, the iterations are won in the details: one counter-example dialogue is often worth more than ten abstract rules.

title: 4  Designing an AI tutor
text:
4.4 Detecting a false (or harmful) answer

Cross-check sources: compare the tutor’s answer with the official documentation (e.g., docs.python.org), other resources, or a small execution test.
Test the code: never copy code without understanding it or running it.
Ask for reasons: a good tutor must be able to justify itself; if it contradicts itself or digs its heels in, you have likely detected the error.
Document: every false answer detected and corrected goes into your logbook. That is one of the goals of the module.

title: 4  Designing an AI tutor
text:
4.5 Typical exercise (block 2)

Choose a simple concept from the module (e.g., the difference between thread and process, or what a coroutine is).
Write a v1 of the system prompt in 5 blocks (role, method, anti-cheating, hallucinations, tone).
Test it on 3 questions: “give me the answer” (the tutor must refuse), “correct my code” (it must make you think), “explain this concept” (it must support without giving everything).
Note 2 observed flaws and propose 2 concrete changes to the prompt.
Keep the v1 of the prompt: it will be attached to your learning plan and discussed at the validation (session 5).

title: 4  Designing an AI tutor
text:
4.6 Self-assessment grid for a prompt

Does the tutor refuse direct requests for the solution?
Does it ask questions that move you forward, rather than closed dead-end questions?
Does it adapt its help if you are lost?
Does it flag its uncertainty instead of making things up?
Does it check understanding before moving to the next point?
Is the tone supportive and the format readable?

title: 5  Planning your learning
text:
5.1 Why a plan?
Learning autonomously without a plan is navigating without a map: you skim and drift, and you never know when you are done. A learning plan (inspired by learning contracts) turns intention into commitment: objectives, an order, success criteria, a schedule. The plan is validated in session 5: it is your roadmap for block 5.

title: 5  Planning your learning
text:
5.2 What the plan must contain

5.2.1 1. Objectives (per technical module)
For each of the 6 modules (async, IPC/locks, distributed, SIMD, GPU, WebGPU), write 2–3 objectives as observable criteria:

“I am able to write a program using asyncio.gather to parallelize I/O and to explain when it speeds things up (and when it does not).”

Avoid vague wording (“understand asyncio”). An objective must allow a yes or no answer: “I can do it without help.”


5.2.2 2. Sequencing

Order of the modules (recommended: async → IPC/locks → distributed → SIMD → GPU → WebGPU) and justification of your order if you change it.
Breakdown: for each module, 2–4 steps with a time estimate.



5.2.3 3. Success criteria and evidence

How will you know the objective is reached? (a successful exercise, a mini-project, an oral or written explanation, a quiz…)
Track A: a conversation with the tutor that shows mastery (e.g. an exercise carried through without the tutor giving away the answer).
Track B: an exercise done alone, ready to be live-coded in front of the instructor.



5.2.4 4. Follow-up schedule
Spread the work between the follow-up points (sessions 6, 7, 8) and the autonomous periods. Plan for slack: the last third of the time stays available for the unexpected and for review.


5.2.5 5. Contract
A short commitment section: your working arrangements (hours, environment, communication channel with the instructor), your “warning signals” (when to ask for help), and any personal adaptations.

5.4 Validation flow (session 5)

Your plan is reviewed individually (~15 min with the instructor).
Track A: the v1 of your system prompt is tested on a simple exercise; the tutor must already “behave” (refuse the solution, guide).
The requested adjustments are to be carried over into the plan; it then becomes your reference for block 5.

title: 5  Planning your learning
6  Introduction to Parallelism
text:
6.1 Notions to master
Introductory module: common to both tracks, covered at the start of the semester. It provides the vocabulary used everywhere else. Full resource: chapter 02_Parallel-intro.qmd from last year’s course; use it as-is or have your AI tutor “teach” it to you.

title: 6  Introduction to Parallelism
text:
Notion
Short definition




Task
a command or a group of commands to run


Worker
a program or subprogram that executes tasks (thread, process)


Resource
unit of computation (CPU core, GPU, remote machine)


Input / Output (I/O)
data needed by a task / results produced


Memory / storage
where the data lives


Synchronization
ordering constraint between tasks (the output of one task is the input of another)

title: 6  Introduction to Parallelism
text:
6.2 Structuring questions

Sequential vs parallel: n tasks, 1 worker → time \sim O(n).
Simple parallel: n tasks, p \ge n workers → time \sim O(1) (bottleneck: not enough workers).
Scheduling: p < n tasks per worker → time \sim O(n/p).
Shared resources: several workers on the same resource → waiting, risk of saturation (organizing the access costs time).
I/O: data not ready / results not written → workers wait; concurrent memory access → bottleneck.


Experiment to redo: the time vs number-of-workers curve is never linear. Go back to last year’s illustrations and interpret the loss (scheduling overhead, I/O, memory).

title: 6  Introduction to Parallelism
text:
6.3 Laws and taxonomy

Amdahl’s law: speedup bounded by the sequential fraction (strong scaling, fixed-size problem):
S_{up}(N) \le \frac{1}{S + \frac{P}{N}}
Gustafson’s law: when the problem size grows with the number of units (weak scaling), the speedup can stay nearly linear.
Flynn’s taxonomy: SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD relate the level of parallelism (instruction, thread, task) to hardware and software.
Multi-processing vs multi-threading: exclusive vs shared memory, inter-process communication vs in-process calls, creation cost, concurrency level (OS vs library/language).

title: 6  Introduction to Parallelism
text:
6.4 Exercises

A program spends 80% of its time in a parallelizable part. Compute the maximum speedup with 2, 4, 16 cores (Amdahl’s law). Interpret.
On your machine: python computes a sum element by element (mentally SISD), then numpy vectorizes. Time n=10^6, 10^7, 10^8. Comment on the gain and why.
Explain in 5 lines the thread/process difference to your AI tutor (Track A) or in your logbook (Track B), then validate with an official resource.

title: 7  Module 1 — Asynchronous and Concurrency
text:
7.1 Key points
Objectives (observable criteria):
Resources: chapter 03_Asynchronous.qmd from last year’s course; official documentation asyncio.

title: 7  Module 1 — Asynchronous and Concurrency
text:
Coroutine: a function declared async def; its execution does not start at the call, you must await it or schedule it.
Event loop: the “conductor” that switches between coroutines when they are waiting (I/O, sleep).
await, asyncio.gather, create_task, asyncio.run.
GIL: Python threads do not compute in parallel on CPU; asyncio is for I/O (network, files, APIs). Do not promise the opposite to your tutor.
Pitfalls: blocking the event loop with a long synchronous call (time.sleep, requests used synchronously); forgetting to await; misusing gather vs create_task.

title: 7  Module 1 — Asynchronous and Concurrency
text:
7.2 Exercises

Download N URLs sequentially, then with asyncio.gather. Time both. Why does requests block? What should you use instead (httpx, aiohttp)?
Write a small asynchronous server/client (asyncio.start_server) answering “pong”.
Trap: mix time.sleep(1) and await asyncio.sleep(1) in concurrent tasks. Time it and explain the result (loop blocking).
(Track A) Ask your tutor “when to use threads vs asyncio?” and “why does the GIL not apply to I/O?”. Check the answers against an official source and document any imprecision.

title: 8  Module 2 — IPC & Locks
text:
8.1 Key points
Objectives (observable criteria):
Resources: chapter 04_IPC-and-Locking.qmd from last year’s course; documentation multiprocessing.

title: 8  Module 2 — IPC & Locks
text:
Process: exclusive memory, communication through IPC; started with spawn (default on macOS/Windows) or fork (Linux).
Queues / Pipes: message exchange. Shared memory (Value, Array, shared_memory): shared data, but it must be protected.
Locks: Lock to serialize a critical section (updating a shared counter, writing a file).
Deadlock: two processes waiting on each other; wrongly ordered locking.
Race conditions: the result depends on execution order → why the lock is necessary (counter illustration).

title: 8  Module 2 — IPC & Locks
text:
8.2 Exercises

Shared counter: 8 processes increment a shared-memory counter 100 000 times each. Without a lock → wrong value; with Lock → correct value. Measure the cost of the lock.
Producer/consumer: one process produces integers, another consumes them through a Queue. Test the natural waiting behavior (queue.Empty).
Deadlock: deliberately create a two-resource deadlock, diagnose it (where is the blockage?) then fix the acquisition order.
Pool: compare Pool.imap vs a sequential loop on a CPU-bound computation.
(Track B) Prepare exercise 1 as live-coding; (Track A) have your tutor explain “why is a Lock necessary if the memory is shared” and assess the accuracy of the explanation.

title: 9  Module 3 — Distributed Computing
text:
9.1 Key points
Objectives (observable criteria):
Resources: chapters 05_Distributed.qmd, 06_Dask-Ray.qmd and 07_Dask-delayed.qmd from last year’s course; official documentation dask and Ray.

title: 9  Module 3 — Distributed Computing
text:
MapReduce / Split-Apply-Combine: break the problem into chunks (split), process each chunk independently (map/apply), then merge the partial results (reduce/combine). Canonical application: word count.
Dask resembles numpy/pandas but lazy: delayed, bag, dataframe, array build a task graph; nothing runs before .compute(). Scheduler (threads, processes, distributed).
dask.delayed: turns a function into a task evaluated lazily; the graph nests and .compute() orchestrates the dependencies.
Ray: actor model, state preserved between calls (@ray.remote on a class), plus futures; designed for stateful services and large-scale parallelism.
delayed best practices: call delayed on the function, not on the result; do not mutate inputs; avoid global state and side effects; split into small tasks but not too small; do not use delayed inside an already-delayed function; do not apply delayed to other Dask collections.
Pitfalls: data serialization between workers (pickle), saturated scheduler, lazy vs eager confusion (forgetting .compute()), too many tiny tasks (scheduling overhead).

title: 9  Module 3 — Distributed Computing
text:
9.2 Exercises

Distributed word count: count the words of a set of text files with dask.bag (map + foldby, or the equivalent), then with a list of files and delayed. Compare times on a single file, then on several.
Lazy pipeline: write 3–4 functions (read → clean → compute → aggregate), chain them with delayed, check that no computation happens before .compute() (how can you tell?), then trigger it.
Dask vs Ray: the same computation (sum of numbers, or incrementing a counter) written with Dask, then with Ray (@ray.remote + actor). Compare the paradigms: graph vs state.
Best practices: start from a delayed function that mutates a global list or a shared array, show the bug (result that depends on order), then fix it by returning the values. Justify the fix.
(Track A) Have your tutor explain “why should you not call delayed on other Dask collections?” and “what is the difference between threads and processes for the scheduler?”. Check each answer against the official documentation. (Track B) Prepare a mini live-coding: turn a sequential loop into a Dask graph, show the gain, and the case where Dask brings nothing.

title: 10  Module 4 — SIMD and Vectorization
text:
10.1 Key points
Objectives (observable criteria):
Resources: chapter 08_SIMD.qmd from last year’s course; documentation numba and numpy.

title: 10  Module 4 — SIMD and Vectorization
text:
Why vectorize? one instruction decoded and executed for multiple data → less decoding, fewer loop iterations, better throughput. A form of instruction-level parallelism, invisible at the thread level.
SIMD registers: SSE (128 bits ≈ 4 32-bit floats), AVX (256 bits ≈ 8 floats), AVX-512; lengths that have grown over time. Consistent with the Flynn taxonomy (intro module): this is data parallelism.
numpy vectorizes: ufuncs (+, *, np.sqrt, np.sum…) operate on the array in one block; data must be contiguous (C-contiguous) to be efficient.
numba: @njit compiles the function to machine code on the first call (just-in-time compilation); parallel=True + prange distributes the iterations; fastmath=True relaxes IEEE arithmetic (always check the impact on precision).
When it is not efficient: small data (call overhead dominates), non-contiguous access, divergent branches, computations where the bottleneck is memory rather than computation.
Intrinsics (C/C++): functions mapping to SIMD instructions (_mm_add_ps, _mm256_fma_ps…); useful to know in order to understand, not needed in Python.

title: 10  Module 4 — SIMD and Vectorization
text:
10.2 Exercises

Loop vs numpy: compute y = 3x^2 + 2 for n = 10^5, 10^6, 10^7, 10^8 in pure Python loop, then with a numpy expression. Plot the time ratio. Why does the gain depend on n?
numba: rewrite the loop from exercise 1 with @njit, then @njit(parallel=True) and prange. Compare with numpy and with the pure loop. What happens at the first call (compilation)?
ufunc and contiguity: time an operation on a contiguous array vs a non-contiguous one (e.g. a view a[::2]). Interpret with the notion of cache.
Non-vectorizable case: write a function with a branch (like collatz or a piecewise function) and compare the approaches. Does vectorization help as much? Why?
(Track A) Ask your tutor “why is numpy faster than a Python loop?” then “what is fastmath and what are the risks?”. Validate against the official docs and document any approximation. (Track B) Prepare a comparative loop/numpy/numba live-coding and explain the result graph.

title: 11  Module 5 — GPU
text:
11.1 Key points
Objectives (observable criteria):
Resources: chapter 09_GPU-Caching-etc.qmd from last year’s course; documentation cupy and numba CUDA.

title: 11  Module 5 — GPU
text:
Architecture: a GPU is massively parallel (thousands of simple cores, throughput-oriented) while a CPU has few complex cores, latency-oriented. The GPU trades control for arithmetic power: threads are numerous, simple, synchronized in batches.
Latency vs throughput: a single GPU thread is slow; performance comes from many operations in flight at the same time. Course metaphors: processing a single order (latency) vs filling the pipeline without interruption (throughput).
Memory: copying between CPU and GPU goes through the bus (PCIe or unified memory) → transfers are expensive: minimize round trips, reuse buffers, do as much computation as possible on the GPU side.
GPU memory hierarchy: registers (fast, scarce) → shared memory (per block, very fast) → global memory (slow); bank conflicts, coalescing to know on a second read.
In Python:

CuPy: cupy.array, cupy.sum, … API modeled on numpy; an array is created on GPU, operations stay there.
numba-CUDA: @cuda.jit defines a kernel; you specify the grid of blocks and threads (cuda.jit([...])(...)), you access the indices (cuda.grid).

Pitfalls: forgetting to synchronize (wrong timing), measuring including the transfer, ignoring the first launch (JIT/JIT-cache compilation), overusing global memory without reuse.

title: 11  Module 5 — GPU
text:
11.2 Exercises

CuPy vs numpy: addition of two large vectors (n = 10^7, 10^8): (a) numpy on CPU,

CuPy measuring everything (transfers included), (c) CuPy measuring only the GPU computation (with cp.cuda.Stream(): and stream.synchronize()). Explain the gaps.

numba-CUDA kernel: write a @cuda.jit vector-addition kernel, launch it on a suitable grid (block size), compare with CuPy. Compute the number of blocks needed to cover n.
Latency vs throughput: build a demonstration (diagram or analogy of your choice: toll booth, pizzas, assembly line) and make a peer or your tutor understand it. Formalize in 3 sentences why more concurrency hides latency.
Transfers: a computation chaining 20 small GPU operations with a copy between each (numpy/CPU loop) vs the same keeping everything on GPU. Measure. Conclusion?
(Track A) Have your tutor explain “why is a GPU slow on a single thread but fast on many?” and “when is it better to stay on CPU?”. Compare with the resources and note the imprecisions. (Track B) Prepare a live-coding: show the cost of a CPU→GPU→CPU round trip on a small operation.

title: 12  Module 6 — WebGPU
text:
12.1 Key points
Objectives (observable criteria):
Resources: chapters 10_WebGPU-First-App.qmd and 11_1_WebGPU-matmul.qmd from last year’s course; official documentation WebGPU and WGSL.

title: 12  Module 6 — WebGPU
text:
WebGPU: a JavaScript API that exposes the GPU to the browser (the replacement of WebGL for computation); you write compute shaders in WGSL, a language close to Rust/C; no native driver to install, a recent browser is enough.
Basic pipeline: navigator.gpu.requestAdapter() → requestDevice() → device.createBuffer() → createBindGroup() → createComputePipeline() → you encode a compute pass → device.queue.submit(). Buffers are typed, aligned, with explicit usage flags.
WGSL: @compute, @workgroup_size, variables in storage or uniform memory, mathematical functions; workgroups / invocations management analogous to CUDA blocks/threads (module 5).
Exemplary math: matrix multiplication (matmul) is the classic benchmark; you compare naive and tiled (per-block reuse) versions on the GPU.
Limits: bound by the GPU, no long-running massive computation (browser session), CPU↔︎GPU transfers always present; the same throughput questions as in module 5, but inside a web page.

title: 12  Module 6 — WebGPU
text:
12.2 Exercises

First app: create a minimal page that initializes WebGPU, writes a constant into a storage buffer through a compute shader, and reads the result in JS to display it. Reuse last year’s template.
Matmul (naive): write a WGSL matmul shader (two matrices passed in storage), compute the product on GPU, compare the result with numpy.dot and measure the time.
Matmul (tiled): write a “tiled” version that reuses blocks via var<workgroup> (local shared memory). Compare with the naive version and explain the gain, if any.
Platform choice: on the same computation (512×512 matmul), compare (a) WebGPU in the browser, (b) CuPy/numba on your GPU, (c) numpy on CPU. What criteria make you choose one or the other?
(Track A) Have your tutor explain “what is a workgroup and what is a workgroup’s shared memory for?” and validate the answer against the WGSL spec. (Track B) Prepare a live-coding: launch the naive WebGPU matmul, show the result and one limit (max workgroup size, performance vs CuPy).

title: 13  Final project
text:
13.1 Framework
The final project counts for 30% of the grade, with the same rubric for both tracks. It assesses the technical mastery of the module’s skills on a concrete problem, mixing several techniques seen in class (asyncio, multiprocessing, Dask, GPU depending on the topic).

title: 13  Final project
text:
Alone or in a pair (communication arrangements chosen by the pair).
Duration: from the launch (end of October) to the defense on 18/11; the report is handed in before the defense.
Common constraints: the project must actually use parallelism (not disguised sequential code), the gains must be measured and justified, and the code must be reproducible (readable README, demonstration script).

title: 13  Final project
text:
13.2 Proposed topics
Each topic is an entry point; you can adapt it or propose another one, as long as it covers the module’s technical objectives.

13.2.1 1. Parallel ETL pipeline
Collect (extraction), clean/merge (transformation), then load data to a target format (CSV, Parquet, SQLite database).

Extraction: concurrent retrieval of sources (paginated APIs, files), with asyncio + httpx.
Transformation: cleaning, aggregations, joins, with multiprocessing, dask or vectorized numpy depending on the data shape.
Loading: writing in Parquet/SQLite; analysis of the impact of parallelism at each step.
Deliverable: a pipeline replayable with a single command, with sequential vs parallel time.



13.2.2 2. OLAP analysis / multidimensional aggregation
Load a dataset (for example ~1 GB of table-typed data, star schema or logs) and prepare aggregations (roll-up, drill-down, cube) used to answer business questions.

Implemented with dask.dataframe / dask.delayed, or cupy/GPU if the hardware allows; comparison with pure pandas.
Deliverable: a “questions → queries → timing visualization” notebook and a report on partitioning strategies.



13.2.3 3. Document retrieval agent (deep research)
An agent that queries several sources simultaneously (web pages, APIs, databases), extracts relevant information, aggregates an argued synthesis and cites its sources.

Collection: concurrent I/O (asyncio, httpx, queues).
Processing: splitting into tasks (dask.delayed) for cleaning and extraction of relevant snippets; LLM-assisted synthesis (optional, not graded per se).
Deliverable: the agent answers a given question, with traceability (sources, time per step) and evidence of the concurrency gain of the collection.



13.2.4 4. Stream processing
Produce a mini continuous-processing system: a producer generates events (logs, simulated sensors), a pipeline aggregates by sliding windows, a consumer displays or stores the results.

Architecture: asyncio (queues, asyncio.Queue) for production/consumption, or multiprocessing + Queue; managing order and backpressure.
Deliverable: a demo showing statistics updating continuously, an architecture diagram and an analysis of the concurrency choices.

title: 13  Final project
text:
13.3 Minimal specification

Clean Git repository: readable history, no large data in the repository.
README: objective, installation (pinned dependencies), launch command, sample output.
Runnable code: main script + minimal tests (at least one unit test on a key function).
Measurements: at least one comparative table (sequential vs parallel, or worker variants) and the interpretation in 3–5 lines.
Report (4–6 pages): objectives, architecture (diagram), technical choices, measurements, limits, what was learned.

13.5 Defense (S11, 18/11, 13:30–15:30)

5–8 minute presentation + questions: what the project does, how it is parallelized, what gains were measured, what limits remain.
The report is submitted before the session. Alternative arrangements (individual session, video submission) are planned if needed.

title: 13  Final project
text:
13.6 Frequently asked questions

Can I use one more library? Yes, as long as the module’s technical subject (asyncio, IPC, Dask, vectorization, GPU/WebGPU depending on the topic) stays the justified core.
What if my hardware has no GPU? GPU topics are optional; an asyncio/Dask/numpy vectorization project is more than enough. The kick-off survey is precisely used to calibrate these choices.
Does the pair count? The level of expectation is adjusted (a more ambitious collective deliverable, or two clearly separated contributions); the roles are spelled out in the report.

title: 14  Module summary
text:
14.1 The thread: parallelism is not free
This page recaps the thread of the module and serves as a navigation map for the autonomous work. It complements the modules: it helps you situate each concept.
The single theme of the course fits in one sentence: parallelizing means decomposing to speed up, but every decomposition has a cost (scheduling, communication, memory, synchronization). The speed curve is never linear in the number of workers.

title: 14  Module summary
text:
14.3 Cross-cutting watch points

Python’s GIL only blocks threads on CPU-bound work; asyncio is for I/O, multiprocessing is for CPU-bound work.
Always measure before and after: only timing (with the cost of transfers for the GPU) justifies an architecture choice.
A lock serializes a critical section: it prevents races but introduces waiting and a risk of deadlock.
Shared state is the enemy of parallelism: prefer pure tasks (no mutation, no side effects) as recommended by Dask best practices.

14.5 Where to start

Read the teaching design (teaching-design.qmd): it is the framework, everything follows from it.

Module 0 first, then M1 → M2 → M3, and depending on your objectives M4 → M5 → M6.

title: 15  References
text:
15.1 Why this design: theoretical framework
The references below ground the module’s pedagogical design (see teaching-design.qmd and ai-tutor.qmd). They are given to help you situate the course; none needs to be read fully to succeed, but each can inform a part of your reflexive report.

title: 15  References
text:
Co-constructed learning: knowledge is built in interaction [1], and students take part in designing their own track [2]–[4], in the tradition of critical pedagogy [5].
Learning contracts: how to write objectives, sequencing and success criteria; the Waterloo Centre for Teaching Excellence factsheet [6].
Learning by teaching with AI: teaching an agent structures learning [7]; conversational tutoring best practices preserve the student’s agency and integrate knowledge tracing [8]; a randomized trial (N=194) suggests that well-designed AI tutoring can outperform active learning in class [9]; a result to be confirmed.
Dialogue and reflexivity: dialogic pedagogy applied to LLMs [10].

title: 15  References
section: 15.2 Documented limits of AI in education
text:
15.2 Documented limits of AI in education
The module treats these limits as objects of work, not taboos:

Hallucinations and reinforcement of misconceptions [11].
Over-reliance and risk of losing basic skills [12]; cognitive offloading and “cognitive debt” [13], [14]; instrumental trust in an assistant [15].
Often superficial student uses [16] and adoption conditioned by trust and institutional policy [17], [18].
Resistance, access inequalities and postures toward technology [19], [20]; student viewpoints [21]; state of the art of pedagogical agents [22].
For those interested in technique as individuation and not merely a tool: [23].

title: 15  References
text:
15.3 Official technical resources
The primary reference for the technique remains the official documentation; your tutor (Track A) and your own research (Track B) must always be checkable against it.

Asynchronous Python: asyncio [24].
Multiprocess and IPC: multiprocessing [25].
Distributed computing: Dask delayed [26] and Ray [27].
Vectorization: numpy ufunc [28] and numba [29].
GPU: CuPy [30] and numba CUDA [29].
WebGPU: WebGPU specification [31] and the WGSL language [32].
